subject.algebraic-geometry.title: Algebraic geometry
subject.algebraic-geometry.define: Commutative algebra, varieties and schemes, followed by local properties, divisors and cohomology of curves.
subject.algebraic-geometry.scope: Selected advanced-undergraduate and beginning-graduate core with advanced gateways. Entries give precise scoped statements and proof ideas, not full proofs or exhaustive courses.
subject.algebraic-geometry.assumed_background: Commutative algebra, modules and tensor products, elementary topology and field extensions.
subject.algebraic-geometry.learning_outcomes:
- Translate geometry into coordinate rings and local rings.
- Retain generic points and nilpotents when passing from varieties to schemes.
- Use divisors, line bundles and cohomology with smoothness and properness hypotheses.

ag.rings.title: Commutative rings, ideals and modules
ag.rings.define: All rings here are commutative with identity and maps preserve identity. An ideal absorbs multiplication by ring elements; a module is the corresponding linear structure with scalars in a ring.
ag.rings.statement: All rings here are commutative with identity and maps preserve identity. An ideal absorbs multiplication by ring elements; a module is the corresponding linear structure with scalars in a ring.
ag.rings.hypotheses: A prime ideal is proper with domain quotient; a maximal ideal has field quotient.
ag.rings.example: $(x)$ is prime in $k[x,y]$, whereas $(x,y)$ is maximal.
ag.rings.caution: A module need not have a basis, and prime ideals need not be maximal.
ag.rings.prerequisites:
**From other subjects**

- [Normal subgroups and quotients](./notes/gt.quotients.md) — Group theory
ag.rings.references:
CAALG: rings, ideals and modules.

- **CAALG** — J. S. Milne. [A Primer of Commutative Algebra](https://www.jmilne.org/math/xnotes/ca.html). Author's course notes.

ag.noetherian.title: Noetherian rings and Hilbert basis theorem
ag.noetherian.define: A ring is Noetherian exactly when every ideal is finitely generated. If A is Noetherian, its polynomial ring in finitely many variables is Noetherian.
ag.noetherian.statement: A ring is Noetherian exactly when every ideal is finitely generated. If A is Noetherian, its polynomial ring in finitely many variables is Noetherian.
ag.noetherian.hypotheses: The equivalence uses the ascending chain condition on ideals.
ag.noetherian.example: Every finitely generated algebra over a field is Noetherian.
ag.noetherian.caution: A polynomial ring in infinitely many variables over a field is not Noetherian.
ag.noetherian.proof_idea: Control leading coefficients in an ascending chain of polynomial ideals and reduce degrees inductively.
ag.noetherian.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Commutative rings, ideals and modules](./notes/ag.rings.md)
ag.noetherian.references:
CAALG: Noetherian rings.

- **CAALG** — J. S. Milne. [A Primer of Commutative Algebra](https://www.jmilne.org/math/xnotes/ca.html). Author's course notes.

ag.localization.title: Localization and local rings
ag.localization.define: Localization inverts selected ring elements and focuses algebra near a prime ideal.
ag.localization.statement: For a multiplicative subset S, $S^{-1}A$ universally makes elements of S invertible. Localizing at $S=A\setminus\mathfrak p$ gives the local ring $A_{\mathfrak p}$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak p A_{\mathfrak p}$.
ag.localization.hypotheses: A local ring has a unique maximal ideal; localization may be the zero ring if zero lies in S.
ag.localization.example: $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$ consists of rationals whose denominators are not divisible by p.
ag.localization.caution: Localization and quotient impose different operations: inversion versus setting elements equal to zero.
ag.localization.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Commutative rings, ideals and modules](./notes/ag.rings.md)
ag.localization.references:
CAALG: localization.

- **CAALG** — J. S. Milne. [A Primer of Commutative Algebra](https://www.jmilne.org/math/xnotes/ca.html). Author's course notes.

ag.nullstellensatz.title: Hilbert Nullstellensatz
ag.nullstellensatz.define: Over an algebraically closed field, polynomial zero sets correspond to radical ideals.
ag.nullstellensatz.statement: Over an algebraically closed field k, maximal ideals of $k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ are point ideals and $I(V(I))=\sqrt I$.
ag.nullstellensatz.hypotheses: The field must be algebraically closed; the number of variables is finite.
ag.nullstellensatz.example: Over $\mathbb C$, the ideal $(x^2)$ and its radical $(x)$ have the same zero set.
ag.nullstellensatz.caution: Point sets alone do not retain nilpotent structure.
ag.nullstellensatz.proof_idea: Zariski's lemma proves the maximal-ideal statement; the Rabinowitsch trick deduces the radical statement.
ag.nullstellensatz.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Noetherian rings and Hilbert basis theorem](./notes/ag.noetherian.md)

- **CAALG** — J. S. Milne. [A Primer of Commutative Algebra](https://www.jmilne.org/math/xnotes/ca.html). Author's course notes.

ag.affine.title: Affine varieties and coordinate rings
ag.affine.define: Affine geometry is encoded contravariantly by coordinate rings.
ag.affine.statement: For an affine algebraic set X over an algebraically closed field, $k[X]=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I(X)$. Regular maps correspond contravariantly to k-algebra homomorphisms of coordinate rings.
ag.affine.hypotheses: Here variety means a reduced irreducible finite-type object, so its coordinate ring is a domain; reducible algebraic sets are also allowed when named as such.
ag.affine.example: The affine parabola has coordinate ring $k[x,y]/(y-x^2)\cong k[x]$.
ag.affine.caution: A polynomial expression in chosen coordinates is a presentation, not the intrinsic object.
ag.affine.references:
AG: affine varieties.

- **AG** — J. S. Milne. [Algebraic Geometry](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/AG.pdf). Version 6.10, 2024.

ag.spec.title: Prime spectrum and Zariski topology
ag.spec.define: The prime spectrum equips all prime ideals with the Zariski topology.
ag.spec.statement: $\operatorname{Spec}A$ is the set of prime ideals, with closed subsets $V(I)=\{\mathfrak p:I\subseteq\mathfrak p\}$. Basic opens $D(f)$ consist of primes not containing f.
ag.spec.hypotheses: All prime ideals are retained, including nonmaximal generic points.
ag.spec.example: $\operatorname{Spec}\mathbb Z$ has closed points (p) and a generic point (0).
ag.spec.caution: The Zariski topology is usually not Hausdorff.
ag.spec.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Commutative rings, ideals and modules](./notes/ag.rings.md)

**From other subjects**

- [Topological spaces and continuity](./notes/tp.spaces.md) — Topology

ag.sheaves.title: Sheaves and stalks
ag.sheaves.define: A sheaf assigns data to open sets with restriction maps, uniqueness of gluing and existence of gluing for compatible local sections. A stalk records germs near one point.
ag.sheaves.statement: A sheaf assigns data to open sets with restriction maps, uniqueness of gluing and existence of gluing for compatible local sections. A stalk records germs near one point.
ag.sheaves.hypotheses: Both gluing axioms distinguish a sheaf from a general presheaf.
ag.sheaves.example: Smooth functions form a sheaf; constant sections require sheafification to capture locally constant functions.
ag.sheaves.caution: Exactness of sheaves is checked on stalks, while taking global sections need not preserve surjections.
ag.sheaves.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Commutative rings, ideals and modules](./notes/ag.rings.md)

**From other subjects**

ag.schemes.title: Schemes and structure sheaves
ag.schemes.define: Schemes glue affine spectra with their sheaves of local algebraic functions.
ag.schemes.statement: A scheme is a locally ringed space locally isomorphic to $(\operatorname{Spec}A,\mathcal O)$, where $\mathcal O(D(f))=A_f$ and the stalk at $\mathfrak p$ is $A_{\mathfrak p}$.
ag.schemes.hypotheses: Morphisms of locally ringed spaces induce local homomorphisms on stalks.
ag.schemes.example: $\operatorname{Spec}k[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$ is a one-point scheme with nontrivial infinitesimal structure.
ag.schemes.caution: The underlying topological space does not determine its scheme structure.
ag.schemes.prerequisites:

ag.morphisms.title: Scheme morphisms and fiber products
ag.morphisms.define: Fiber products express base change and are built affinely by tensor products.
ag.morphisms.statement: A ring map $A\to B$ induces $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A$. Fiber products satisfy the universal property of simultaneous maps and, affinely, use tensor products: $\operatorname{Spec}B\times_{\operatorname{Spec}A}\operatorname{Spec}C=\operatorname{Spec}(B\otimes_A C)$.
ag.morphisms.hypotheses: The base scheme and structure morphisms are part of the data.
ag.morphisms.example: Extension of the ground field is base change.
ag.morphisms.caution: Topological fiber products alone lose the structure sheaf and multiplicities.
ag.morphisms.references:
STACKS: morphisms and fiber products.

- **STACKS** — The Stacks Project Authors. [The Stacks Project](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/browse). Living reference; schemes, morphisms and algebraic curves.

ag.projective.title: Projective space and Proj
ag.projective.define: Proj constructs projective geometry from graded commutative algebra.
ag.projective.statement: Projective n-space over A is $\operatorname{Proj}A[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$. For a nonnegatively graded ring S, Proj uses homogeneous prime ideals not containing the irrelevant ideal $S_+$.
ag.projective.hypotheses: Its standard affine charts use degree-zero parts of homogeneous localizations.
ag.projective.example: Homogeneous equations define projective subschemes, including a smooth plane cubic.
ag.projective.caution: Homogeneous coordinates are defined up to simultaneous nonzero scaling over a field.
ag.projective.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

ag.dimension.title: Dimension and Noether normalization
ag.dimension.define: A finitely generated integral k-algebra A is finite over a polynomial subalgebra in d algebraically independent elements. Its Krull dimension equals d and equals the transcendence degree of its fraction field over k.
ag.dimension.statement: A finitely generated integral k-algebra A is finite over a polynomial subalgebra in d algebraically independent elements. Its Krull dimension equals d and equals the transcendence degree of its fraction field over k.
ag.dimension.hypotheses: A is a domain of finite type over a field.
ag.dimension.example: An irreducible plane curve has dimension one.
ag.dimension.caution: Embedding dimension, tangent-space dimension and Krull dimension need not coincide at singular points.
ag.dimension.proof_idea: Choose a change of generators making one algebraic relation monic, then induct on the number of generators.
ag.dimension.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Noetherian rings and Hilbert basis theorem](./notes/ag.noetherian.md)
- [Affine varieties and coordinate rings](./notes/ag.affine.md)

ag.regular.title: Regularity and smoothness
ag.regular.define: Regular local rings compare dimension with tangent size; smoothness is relative.
ag.regular.statement: A Noetherian local ring is regular when $\dim A=\dim_{\kappa}(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2)$. For a finite-type scheme over a perfect field, regularity is equivalent to smoothness over that field.
ag.regular.hypotheses: Smoothness is a relative notion; the perfect-field hypothesis matters for this comparison.
ag.regular.example: The cusp has a larger tangent space than its local dimension at the singular point.
ag.regular.caution: Over an imperfect field, regular need not mean geometrically regular or smooth over that field.
ag.regular.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Dimension and Noether normalization](./notes/ag.dimension.md)
- [Localization and local rings](./notes/ag.localization.md)

ag.proper.title: Proper and projective morphisms
ag.proper.define: A proper morphism is separated, of finite type and universally closed. A projective morphism factors as a closed immersion into a finite-dimensional projective space over the base and is proper.
ag.proper.statement: A proper morphism is separated, of finite type and universally closed. A projective morphism factors as a closed immersion into a finite-dimensional projective space over the base and is proper.
ag.proper.hypotheses: Universal closedness means closedness after every base change.
ag.proper.example: Projective space is proper over its ground field; affine space of positive dimension is not.
ag.proper.caution: Proper need not mean projective, and topological compactness is not the definition.
ag.proper.prerequisites:

ag.flat.title: Flatness
ag.flat.define: Flat modules preserve exact sequences under tensoring.
ag.flat.statement: An A-module M is flat if $-\otimes_A M$ preserves exact sequences. A scheme morphism $f:X\to Y$ is flat when $\mathcal O_{X,x}$ is flat over $\mathcal O_{Y,f(x)}$ for every x in X.
ag.flat.hypotheses: For a morphism X to Y, stalks of X are modules over the corresponding stalks of Y.
ag.flat.example: Localizations and free modules are flat.
ag.flat.caution: Flatness alone does not force every fiber to be smooth.
ag.flat.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Localization and local rings](./notes/ag.localization.md)
- [Scheme morphisms and fiber products](./notes/ag.morphisms.md)

ag.etale.title: Étale morphisms
ag.etale.define: An etale morphism is smooth of relative dimension zero, equivalently flat, unramified and locally of finite presentation.
ag.etale.statement: An etale morphism is smooth of relative dimension zero, equivalently flat, unramified and locally of finite presentation.
ag.etale.hypotheses: Etale is a relative condition and includes a finiteness requirement.
ag.etale.example: A finite separable field extension induces an etale map of spectra.
ag.etale.caution: In positive characteristic the Frobenius of an affine line is not etale.
ag.etale.references:
STACKS: etale morphisms.

- **STACKS** — The Stacks Project Authors. [The Stacks Project](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/browse). Living reference; schemes, morphisms and algebraic curves.

ag.divisors.title: Weil and Cartier divisors
ag.divisors.define: On a Noetherian normal integral scheme, a Weil divisor is a finite integral sum of codimension-one integral closed subschemes. A Cartier divisor is locally a nonzero rational function modulo invertible regular functions.
ag.divisors.statement: On a Noetherian normal integral scheme, a Weil divisor is a finite integral sum of codimension-one integral closed subschemes. A Cartier divisor is locally a nonzero rational function modulo invertible regular functions.
ag.divisors.hypotheses: Cartier divisors define Weil divisors in this setting; they coincide on locally factorial schemes, including regular Noetherian integral schemes.
ag.divisors.example: On a smooth curve a divisor is a finite integer-weighted sum of closed points.
ag.divisors.caution: On singular normal varieties, not every Weil divisor is Cartier.
ag.divisors.prerequisites:

ag.line-bundles.title: Line bundles and the Picard group
ag.line-bundles.define: Rank-one locally free sheaves form the Picard group under tensor product.
ag.line-bundles.statement: Invertible sheaves are locally free modules of rank one over the structure sheaf. Tensor product gives their isomorphism classes the group $\operatorname{Pic}(X)$. A Cartier divisor D defines $\mathcal O_X(D)$.
ag.line-bundles.hypotheses: The inverse line bundle is its dual; on an integral scheme Cartier divisors modulo principal divisors give the Picard group.
ag.line-bundles.example: On projective space the bundles $\mathcal O(m)$ measure degree.
ag.line-bundles.caution: A line bundle may be locally trivial but globally nontrivial.
ag.line-bundles.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Weil and Cartier divisors](./notes/ag.divisors.md)

ag.cohomology.title: Sheaf cohomology
ag.cohomology.define: Sheaf cohomology measures the failure of global sections to preserve exactness.
ag.cohomology.statement: Sheaf cohomology $H^i(X,\mathcal F)$ is the right derived functor of global sections. For affine X and quasi-coherent $\mathcal F$, $H^i(X,\mathcal F)=0$ for $i>0$.
ag.cohomology.hypotheses: The vanishing statement is for quasi-coherent sheaves, not arbitrary sheaves; derived functors are taken in the abelian sheaf category.
ag.cohomology.example: Cohomology measures obstructions to solving gluing problems globally.
ag.cohomology.caution: A single arbitrary Cech cover does not always compute derived-functor cohomology.
ag.cohomology.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Sheaves and stalks](./notes/ag.sheaves.md)
- [Schemes and structure sheaves](./notes/ag.schemes.md)

ag.curves.title: Smooth projective curves and genus
ag.curves.define: The genus of a smooth projective curve is a cohomological invariant.
ag.curves.statement: For a smooth projective geometrically integral curve C over k, its genus is $g=\dim_k H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)$. The canonical line bundle is $\omega_C=\Omega^1_{C/k}$.
ag.curves.hypotheses: Geometric integrality ensures the curve remains integral after field extension.
ag.curves.example: The projective line has genus zero; a smooth plane cubic has genus one.
ag.curves.caution: Arithmetic and geometric genus may differ for singular curves.
ag.curves.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Sheaf cohomology](./notes/ag.cohomology.md)
- [Projective space and Proj](./notes/ag.projective.md)
- [Regularity and smoothness](./notes/ag.regular.md)

ag.riemann-roch.title: Riemann–Roch for curves
ag.riemann-roch.define: Riemann–Roch balances sections, divisor degree and genus on smooth projective curves.
ag.riemann-roch.statement: For a divisor D on a smooth projective geometrically integral curve of genus g over an algebraically closed field, $\ell(D)-\ell(K_C-D)=\deg D+1-g$, where $\ell(D)=\dim H^0(C,\mathcal O_C(D))$.
ag.riemann-roch.hypotheses: K_C is a canonical divisor; degree and genus use the curve's smooth projective structure.
ag.riemann-roch.caution: The same formula without correction does not apply to arbitrary singular or nonproper curves.
ag.riemann-roch.proof_idea: Compute the Euler characteristic by adding points to a divisor and use Serre duality to identify the H1 term.
ag.riemann-roch.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Smooth projective curves and genus](./notes/ag.curves.md)
- [Line bundles and the Picard group](./notes/ag.line-bundles.md)

ag.serre-duality.title: Serre duality on curves
ag.serre-duality.define: The canonical bundle pairs first cohomology with a dual space of sections.
ag.serre-duality.statement: For a line bundle L on a smooth projective geometrically integral curve C over k, $H^1(C,L)$ is naturally dual to $H^0(C,\omega_C\otimes L^{-1})$.
ag.serre-duality.hypotheses: Finite-dimensionality and the dualizing canonical bundle use properness and smoothness in this version.
ag.serre-duality.example: Applying this to the structure sheaf identifies the genus with the dimension of regular differentials.
ag.serre-duality.caution: For singular schemes one needs a dualizing object rather than blindly substituting the sheaf of differentials.
ag.serre-duality.proof_idea: The trace map on H1 of the canonical bundle turns cup product into a perfect pairing.
ag.serre-duality.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Smooth projective curves and genus](./notes/ag.curves.md)
- [Line bundles and the Picard group](./notes/ag.line-bundles.md)
